title: The tyre after a hot drive
hook: A tyre reads 220 kPa when parked. Drive until the air inside is 30 °C warmer. Now what?

knows: that heating a sealed gas raises its pressure
that tyres are checked with a pressure gauge
doesNotKnow: that gas pressure is proportional to temperature counted from absolute zero (kelvin)
that a tyre gauge leaves out the outside air's pressure

misconception: Pressure scales with the Celsius number, so 20 °C to 50 °C makes the gauge 2.5 times higher.
objective: The learner can explain that warming a rigid tyre from 20 °C (293 K) to 50 °C (323 K) raises the total pressure about 10%, from about 321 to 354 kPa, so the gauge goes from 220 to about 253 kPa: a modest 15%, because pressure follows kelvin and the gauge omits the outside 101 kPa.

claims.text: For a fixed amount of gas in a fixed volume, pressure is proportional to temperature in kelvin.
claims.source: Ideal gas law pV = nRT at constant n, V (Gay-Lussac's law); Atkins, Physical Chemistry, ch. 1. Demo.tsx abs(c) = P_ABS0 × (c + 273.15) / 293.15.

claims.text: Kelvin counts from absolute zero: K = °C + 273; 20 °C is 293 K and 50 °C is 323 K.
claims.source: SI: T/K = t/°C + 273.15 (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed.). 293.15 and 323.15 rounded.

claims.text: A tyre gauge shows pressure above the outside air; the outside air at sea level pushes about 101 kPa.
claims.source: Gauge pressure = absolute − atmospheric (NIST SP 811 / any physics text); standard atmosphere 101.325 kPa.

claims.text: Warming the tyre from 20 °C to 50 °C raises the total pressure about 10%, from about 321 to 354 kPa, so the gauge reads about 253 kPa: up about 33 kPa, or 15%.
claims.source: (220 + 101.325) × 323.15 / 293.15 = 354.21 kPa absolute; − 101.325 = 252.88 kPa gauge; 354.21 / 321.325 = 1.102; 252.88 / 220 = 1.149 (node; Demo.tsx HOT_GAUGE). Wrong options: 220 × 50/20 = 550 (Celsius ratio); 354 (forgets to subtract the outside air).

claims.text: The tyre is modelled as an ideal gas in a fixed volume.
claims.source: Model label on the stage ('ideal gas, fixed volume'). Real tyres stretch slightly when warm, so the real rise is a little smaller; air at 3 bar is close to ideal (compressibility factor about 1.00; NIST REFPROP air). Atmospheric pressure assumed 101.325 kPa.

recall.question: A sealed, rigid can of gas at 27 °C (300 K) is heated to 54 °C. Its absolute pressure becomes about…
recall.why: Pressure follows kelvin: 300 K to 327 K is about 9% warmer, so the pressure rises about 9%, not double.
